sections.body: Azure RBAC is built on Azure Resource Manager, spans the control and data planes, and is now both the recommended and (as of API version 2026-02-01) default authorization model for new vaults. It centralizes access management, requires Owner/User Access Administrator rights to grant permissions, and integrates with Privileged Identity Management for time-limited elevated access. The access policy model is a legacy, Key Vault-native, data-plane-only system where individual permissions are assigned per security principal directly on the vault.

sections.heading: SDK clients: SecretClient, KeyClient, CertificateClient
sections.body: Each object type has its own client in `Azure.Security.KeyVault.*`: `SecretClient` for secrets, `KeyClient` for keys, and `CertificateClient` for certificate lifecycle operations (create, list, update, delete, manage issuers/policies). `CertificateClient` is authenticated the same way as other Key Vault clients, typically with `DefaultAzureCredential`, and Microsoft recommends using a managed identity for production authentication.

sections.heading: Getting a certificate's private key (the PFX gotcha)
sections.body: Key Vault keeps a certificate's private key material as a **secret**, not merely as part of the certificate object — this only applies if the certificate was created or imported with an exportable policy. To download the full key pair (e.g., as a PFX) you retrieve it as a secret (via `SecretClient`, or via `CertificateClient.DownloadCertificate`/`DownloadCertificateAsync`, which wraps this for you). Microsoft's own guidance cautions that keeping private-key operations (decrypt, sign, unwrap) inside Key Vault is preferred over exporting the key locally.

articles.title: Managed Identities: System-Assigned vs User-Assigned, and Living with the DefaultAzureCredential Pattern
articles.summary: Learn the practical differences between system-assigned and user-assigned managed identities, how DefaultAzureCredential removes secrets from your code, and the propagation-delay and cross-tenant gotchas that show up on the exam and in production.
keyPoints: A managed identity is a Microsoft Entra identity automatically tied to an Azure compute resource (VM, VMSS, Service Fabric, AKS, or any supported App hosting platform), removing the need to manage credentials in code.
System-assigned identity: created as part of the resource, shares its lifecycle (deleted when the resource is deleted), and cannot be shared across resources.

User-assigned identity: created as a standalone Azure resource with an independent lifecycle, and can be assigned to multiple Azure resources at once — Microsoft calls this the recommended type for services needing a shared/pre-provisioned identity.

Code retrieves a token for a managed identity using the Azure Identity SDK's DefaultAzureCredential (or MSAL), which works unmodified locally (falling back to a developer credential) and in Azure (using ManagedIdentityCredential).
You must still explicitly authorize the managed identity against the target resource (e.g., an RBAC role assignment on a Key Vault or storage account) — a valid token alone won't grant access.

For App Service/Functions, the back-end token cache is keyed per resource URI and cached for around 24 hours; changes to a managed identity's group or role membership can take up to 24 hours to take effect, and there is no way to force an early refresh.

Managed identities don't support cross-directory/tenant scenarios — moving an app's subscription to another tenant does not automatically re-create the managed identity, and downstream resources need their access updated to the new identity.

sections.heading: System-assigned vs user-assigned
sections.body: System-assigned managed identities are tied one-to-one to a resource: enabling one creates a service principal whose lifecycle matches that resource, and it can't be reused elsewhere. User-assigned managed identities are standalone resources you create independently and can attach to many resources — recommended when multiple compute resources need to share one identity, or when you need to pre-authorize access before provisioning the compute resource itself.

sections.heading: The DefaultAzureCredential pattern
sections.body: Application code uses `DefaultAzureCredential` from the Azure Identity library (or MSAL) to acquire a Microsoft Entra token without ever handling a secret. Locally it falls back through credential sources like environment variables, Visual Studio, or shared token cache; when running in Azure with a managed identity assigned, it automatically uses `ManagedIdentityCredential` against the platform's local token endpoint (`IDENTITY_ENDPOINT` / `IDENTITY_HEADER` on App Service and Functions).

sections.heading: Services that support managed identities
sections.body: Managed identities can authenticate to any resource that supports Microsoft Entra authentication, including Azure Key Vault, Azure SQL Database, and Azure Storage — but the target resource must still be explicitly configured (typically via an RBAC role assignment) to allow that identity's access; otherwise the service rejects the request even with a valid token.

sections.heading: Gotchas: propagation delay and tenant moves
sections.body: App Service documentation explicitly warns that its managed-identity token back end caches per resource URI for about 24 hours, so role/group membership changes may take up to 24 hours to take effect, with no way to force a refresh before the cached token expires — plan around this rather than expecting instant propagation after a role assignment. Separately, because managed identities don't support cross-directory scenarios, moving a subscription to a different tenant does not automatically re-create the managed identities, and any downstream resource access policies must be updated to the new identity.

articles.title: Azure App Configuration: Centralized Settings, Feature Flags, and Key Vault References
articles.summary: Understand what Azure App Configuration centralizes versus what belongs in Key Vault, and how a Key Vault reference lets App Configuration point at a secret without ever storing it.
keyPoints: Azure App Configuration centrally manages application settings and feature flags, following the Twelve-Factor App principle of separating configuration from code.
It complements Azure Key Vault rather than replacing it: App Configuration is for general configuration data, Key Vault remains the store for secrets.

Benefits include dynamically changing settings without redeploying/restarting an app, point-in-time replay of settings, labeling, a dedicated feature-flag UI, and enhanced security through Azure managed identities.
A Key Vault reference is a special App Configuration key whose stored value is a URI pointing at a Key Vault secret — not the secret value itself.

App Configuration and Key Vault do not communicate directly with each other; your application authenticates to both separately, and the App Configuration client provider is what recognizes a Key Vault reference and fetches the real value from Key Vault.
Client libraries/providers exist for .NET, ASP.NET Core, .NET Framework, Java Spring, JavaScript/Node.js, Python, and Go, plus a REST API for anything else.
DefaultAzureCredential (backed by a managed identity in Azure) is the recommended way to authenticate to both App Configuration and the referenced Key Vault from the same code.

sections.heading: What App Configuration provides
sections.body: App Configuration is a fully managed service for centralizing configuration and feature flags across distributed components — microservices, serverless apps, or continuous deployment pipelines — so settings don't have to be duplicated or hard-coded per instance. It supports flexible key representations, labels, point-in-time replay, and a dedicated feature-flag management UI.

sections.heading: App Configuration vs Key Vault
sections.body: Microsoft documentation is explicit that App Configuration "complements" Key Vault: use App Configuration for general settings (connection endpoints, feature flags, non-sensitive values) and keep secrets such as connection strings, API keys, or certificates in Key Vault, even when your app resolves them through App Configuration.

sections.heading: Key Vault references
sections.body: When you create a Key Vault reference in App Configuration, the value App Configuration stores is a URI pointing to the secret in Key Vault — never the secret or credential itself. The client provider recognizes that key as a Key Vault reference and retrieves the actual value from Key Vault at read time, the same way it reads any other App Configuration key from the application's perspective.

articles.title: Instrumenting Apps for Application Insights: Connection Strings, Auto-Instrumentation, and Sampling
articles.summary: Covers how to wire an app up to Application Insights today - connection strings, choosing between autoinstrumentation and the OpenTelemetry Distro, setting cloud role name/instance, and configuring sampling.
keyPoints: Use the connection string (not a bare instrumentation key) to point your app at an Application Insights resource - it's a semicolon-separated key-value string (max 4,096 chars) that wraps the instrumentation key and adds endpoint/authentication options.

For code-based server apps (ASP.NET Core, .NET, Java, Node.js, Python, AKS), the recommended setup is the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro; browser apps use the separate Application Insights JavaScript SDK, which does NOT use OpenTelemetry.

Autoinstrumentation (a portal toggle, e.g. for App Service or Azure Functions) requires no code changes and is enabled by default on many platforms; switch to the OpenTelemetry Distro for more configuration/extensibility, or when autoinstrumentation isn't supported (e.g. multi-container/sidecar App Service deployments).

Cloud Role Name comes from the OpenTelemetry resource attributes service.namespace + service.name (falls back to service.name alone if namespace isn't set); Cloud Role Instance comes from service.instance.id.

Sampling in the OpenTelemetry-based distro supports two strategies: fixed-rate/fixed-percentage (e.g. OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=microsoft.fixed_percentage, ratio 0.0-1.0) and rate-limited (microsoft.rate_limited, max traces/sec) - defaults vary by language/SDK version.
Sampling decisions apply only to traces (spans); metrics are never sampled; logs belonging to unsampled traces are dropped by default unless trace-based log sampling is explicitly disabled.
Live Metrics requires Application Insights' own custom sampler for compatibility, which is why the distro ships a built-in sampler rather than relying solely on generic OpenTelemetry samplers.

sections.heading: Connection strings
sections.body: A connection string is the current, recommended way to tell an SDK where to send telemetry. It's a list of `key=value` pairs (e.g. `InstrumentationKey=...;IngestionEndpoint=...`) and can override individual service endpoints (ingestion, live metrics, profiler, snapshot debugger) or an entire endpoint suffix for sovereign clouds. The instrumentation key it contains is not a secret/security token by itself - connection strings add real security value mainly by enabling Microsoft Entra ID-authenticated ingestion.

sections.heading: Choosing an instrumentation approach
sections.body: Entry points differ by hosting model: web apps and VMs use the **Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro** with a connection string; Azure Functions enable OpenTelemetry via `host.json` (`"telemetryMode": "OpenTelemetry"`); browser telemetry uses the JavaScript SDK (not OpenTelemetry). Autoinstrumentation is available as a no-code toggle on select platforms (App Service, Azure Functions, AKS in preview) and is often on by default - move to code-based OpenTelemetry Distro instrumentation when you need custom configuration or when autoinstrumentation isn't supported for your deployment shape.

sections.heading: Cloud role name and cloud role instance
Sampling
sections.body: Sampling controls ingestion volume and cost. The distro's two strategies are **fixed-rate/fixed-percentage** sampling (send a fixed fraction of traces, e.g. `0.1` ≈ 10%) and **rate-limited** sampling (cap traces per second, e.g. `1.5` traces/sec). Configure via environment variables (`OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` = `microsoft.fixed_percentage` or `microsoft.rate_limited`, with `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG`) or in code (`o.SamplingRatio` / `o.TracesPerSecond`). Metrics are never sampled - Microsoft's guidance is to alert on metrics for reliable signals, since sampling only affects traces (and, by default, logs tied to unsampled traces).

articles.title: Application Insights Telemetry Types: Standard vs Log-Based Metrics and Querying with KQL
articles.summary: Explains the difference between fast preaggregated standard metrics and flexible-but-sampling-sensitive log-based metrics, the core telemetry tables, and how KQL is used to query them.
keyPoints: Application Insights supports three metric types: standard (preaggregated), log-based, and custom.

Standard metrics are preaggregated at collection time into a dedicated time-series store with fixed 1-minute granularity; they are NOT affected by sampling and query fast - best for near-real-time alerting and dashboards.

Log-based metrics are a query-time concept: they're computed from raw log data via Kusto queries at query time (no preaggregation), which preserves all log properties as filterable/splittable dimensions but means sampling and telemetry filtering DO reduce their accuracy.

Core telemetry stored as Log Analytics tables includes: requests, dependencies, exceptions, traces, pageViews, customEvents, customMetrics, availabilityResults, browserTimings, and performanceCounters.
Custom metrics are stored in both the metrics store (no dimensions by default; dimensions are a billed preview option) and in full-dimension form in Log Analytics logs.

Azure Monitor Logs (including Application Insights logs) use KQL (Kusto Query Language) - the same language as Azure Data Explorer, though a handful of statements/functions (e.g. cluster(), Python plugin) aren't supported in Azure Monitor.
Log Analytics in the Azure portal is the primary tool to write and interactively test KQL queries, which can then feed log search alert rules, workbooks, and dashboards.

sections.heading: Standard, log-based, and custom metrics compared
sections.body: Standard (platform) metrics are automatically collected and preaggregated during runtime into a specialized time-series store - high accuracy (unaffected by sampling), fast queries, but only key dimensions. Log-based metrics are derived on the fly from stored log/event data using KQL, so they support arbitrary telemetry-field filtering and splitting, but their accuracy is reduced by any sampling or filtering applied upstream, and queries are slower since they scan log data rather than a preaggregated store. Custom metrics are user-defined via the SDK/OpenTelemetry API and are stored in both the metrics store and Log Analytics.

sections.heading: Why the distinction matters for alerting
sections.body: Because log-based metrics can be skewed by sampling, use standard/pre-aggregated metrics when you need reliable near-real-time alerting on volume-sensitive signals (e.g. failed request counts), and reserve log-based metrics for deep diagnostics where you need to slice by arbitrary dimensions rather than raw accuracy.

sections.heading: Core telemetry types
sections.body: The telemetry Application Insights collects and exposes as Log Analytics tables/`itemType` values includes **requests**, **dependencies** (outbound calls to databases/APIs/external services), **exceptions**, **traces** (application logs), **pageViews** and **browserTimings** (client-side, via the JS SDK), **customEvents**/**customMetrics** (manual instrumentation, e.g. `TelemetryClient.TrackEvent()`), and **availabilityResults** (from availability tests).

sections.heading: Querying with KQL
sections.body:
Azure Monitor Logs is built on Azure Data Explorer and uses the same KQL. A typical log-based metric query looks like: ```kusto
requests
| where success == 'False'
| summarize ['requests/failed_sum'] = sum(itemCount) by bin(timestamp, 15m)
| render barchart
``` Log Analytics in the Azure portal is where you author and test these queries before reusing them in log search alert rules, workbooks, or dashboards.

articles.title: Availability Tests and Alert Rules: Standard Tests, the Retiring URL Ping Test, and Action Groups
articles.summary: Explains which availability test type to use now that URL ping tests are being retired, and how Azure Monitor alert rules and action groups turn failures into notifications.
keyPoints: Standard tests are the current recommended availability test type - a single-request test (like the old URL ping test) that adds TLS/SSL certificate validation, proactive certificate-lifetime checks, custom HTTP verb, custom headers, and custom request body.

URL ping tests are deprecated and will be retired on September 30, 2026 - existing URL ping tests will be removed from Application Insights resources after that date; Microsoft publishes a PowerShell-based migration path from URL ping tests to Standard tests.

Custom availability tests built with the TrackAvailability() API are now documented only as archived 'Classic API' guidance for existing implementations - current guidance is to use Standard tests where possible.
You can create up to 100 availability tests per Application Insights resource; a minimum of 5 test locations is recommended so you can distinguish app problems from regional network issues.

Availability alerts are enabled by default and are near-real-time and state-based: you get one email when the endpoint goes down and another when it recovers, not a repeated alert every evaluation cycle.
The recommended alert location threshold is (number of test locations - 2), with a minimum of 5 locations - e.g. 3-of-5 locations reporting failure before alerting.

Azure Monitor alert types include metric alerts, log search alerts, simple log search alerts, activity log alerts, smart detection alerts, and Prometheus alerts; an alert rule combines a target resource, a signal, and a condition, and firing it triggers an action group.

Action groups can notify via email/SMS/push, or trigger automation runbooks, Azure Functions, Logic Apps, ITSM incidents, event hubs, or webhooks; alerts can be stateful (fire once until the condition resolves) or stateless (fire every time the condition is met, as with all activity log alerts).

sections.heading: Standard tests vs the deprecated URL ping test
sections.body: A Standard test sends a single HTTP request, just like a URL ping test, but additionally validates the TLS/SSL certificate (including a proactive check ahead of certificate expiry), and lets you set the HTTP verb, custom headers, and a request body. URL ping tests are deprecated and retire on **September 30, 2026** - after that date they're removed from Application Insights resources, so any team still relying on them needs to migrate before then.

sections.heading: TrackAvailability(): archived Classic API guidance
sections.body: Custom availability tests built by calling `TrackAvailability()` directly are now documented only as archived 'Classic API' material intended for teams that already have such an implementation. Current Microsoft guidance is to use Standard tests for availability monitoring going forward rather than building custom TrackAvailability()-based tests.

sections.heading: Configuring availability alerts
sections.body: Alerts are automatically enabled when you create an availability test, but you must open the associated alert rule and set severity, description, and an action group to actually receive notifications through your configured channels (otherwise you only get in-portal notifications). These automatic alerts are near-real-time and state based - a single alert fires when the site is detected down, and a resolved notification fires once it's back, rather than repeating every evaluation interval. The recommended alert location threshold is **(number of test locations - 2)**, with a minimum of 5 locations.

sections.heading: Alert rules and action groups
sections.body: An Azure Monitor **alert rule** = a monitored resource + a signal/condition; when the condition is met, the alert fires and triggers an **action group** - which can send email/SMS/push notifications or invoke automation runbooks, Azure Functions, Logic Apps, ITSM tools, event hubs, or webhooks. Alert types include metric alerts (evaluate resource/custom/Application Insights metrics, support dynamic thresholds), log search alerts (KQL query evaluated on a schedule), simple log search alerts (evaluate each row individually for near-real-time scale), activity log alerts (fire on management-plane events, always stateless), smart detection alerts (Application Insights anomaly detection), and Prometheus alerts (PromQL-based). Alerts can be stateful - e.g. a metric alert resolves only after 3 consecutive checks don't meet the condition - or stateless, firing every time the condition is met.

articles.title: APIM Building Blocks: Gateway, Products, Subscriptions, and Tiers
articles.summary: Learn how Azure API Management's gateway, products, and subscriptions fit together, and which pricing tier actually supports the self-hosted gateway.
keyPoints: APIM has three components: the API gateway (data plane), the management plane (control plane), and the developer portal
Classic tiers are Developer, Basic, Standard, Premium; V2 tiers are Basic v2, Standard v2, Premium v2; Consumption is a serverless, pay-per-execution tier
Products bundle one or more APIs and are either open (no subscription needed) or protected (subscription key required)
A subscription can be scoped to a product, to all APIs, or to a single API; every instance also has a built-in all-access subscription
The subscription key is sent as the Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key header or the subscription-key query parameter
The self-hosted gateway (containerized gateway) applies to the Developer and Premium tiers, not just Premium
API versions use a path, header, or query-string scheme and are grouped in a version set; versions are distinct from revisions

sections.heading: Gateway, management plane, developer portal
sections.body: The **API gateway** (data plane) sits in front of backend services: it verifies API keys, JWTs, and certificates, enforces quotas and rate limits, applies policies, optionally caches responses, and emits logs/metrics. The **management plane** is what API providers use (Azure portal, CLI, PowerShell, REST API, VS Code extension) to configure the service, import API schemas, package APIs into products, and manage users. The **developer portal** is an automatically generated, customizable site where API consumers discover APIs, try them via an interactive console, and subscribe to get keys.

sections.heading: Pricing tiers
sections.body: Tiers are grouped into three families: **Classic** (Developer, Basic, Standard, Premium - Premium adds private backend access, multi-region deployment, and availability zones; Developer is for non-production use only), **V2** (Basic v2 for dev/test, Standard v2 and Premium v2 for production, both supporting VNet integration, with Premium v2 also supporting VNet injection), and **Consumption**, a serverless gateway that scales on demand and bills per execution.

sections.heading: Products and subscriptions
sections.body: A **product** is how APIs are exposed to consumers; it can be *open* (no subscription required, so it won't even show on the developer portal's Products page) or *protected* (subscription key required). Subscription approval can be automatic or require publisher approval. A subscription's scope can be a product, all APIs, or a single API - API-scoped, all-APIs, and the built-in all-access subscriptions bypass any policies configured at product scope. Regenerate keys using the paired primary/secondary key model to rotate credentials with minimal disruption.

sections.heading: Self-hosted gateway tier availability
sections.body: The self-hosted gateway is an optional, Linux-container version of the managed gateway that you deploy into your own environment (on-premises, another cloud, Kubernetes, or Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes) to reduce latency and meet compliance needs. According to Microsoft's official self-hosted-gateway-overview page, it **applies to the Developer and Premium tiers** - it is available for non-production evaluation on Developer and for production use on Premium, not exclusively Premium as is sometimes assumed. It "fails static" during Azure connectivity loss, continuing to serve traffic from its last known (or backed-up) configuration.

sections.heading: Versioning vs. revisions
sections.body: Versions let you publish multiple, independently evolvable copies of an API (each can have different operations and policies) using a **path**, **header**, or **query-string** versioning scheme; versions belonging to the same logical API are grouped into a **version set**. Adding a version to a previously non-versioned API auto-creates an `Original` version so existing callers are unaffected. Versions are distinct from **revisions**: revisions are for non-breaking changes to the same version, while versions are for breaking changes - a revision can later be promoted into a formal version.

articles.title: APIM Policies: Inbound/Backend/Outbound/On-Error and What Managed Identity Auth Can't Do
articles.summary: Understand the policy XML pipeline, the five policy scopes, and the precise (limited) behavior of the authentication-managed-identity policy.
keyPoints: Policy XML has four sections executed in order: inbound, backend, outbound, on-error
If any error occurs in inbound/backend/outbound, remaining steps there are skipped and execution jumps straight to on-error, where context.LastError is available
Policy scopes, broadest to narrowest: global, workspace, product, API, operation
The <base/> element controls whether and where a scope inherits policies from the parent scope
rate-limit-by-key limits calls per a computed key (not available on Consumption tier); rate-limit/quota policies work per subscription and require a subscription key

authentication-managed-identity fetches a Microsoft Entra ID token via the APIM instance's managed identity and sets it as a Bearer Authorization header - it authenticates APIM to a backend; it does not retrieve a TLS/client certificate from Key Vault
cache-lookup and cache-store implement response caching in the inbound/outbound sections respectively

sections.heading: Policy XML structure
sections.body: A policy definition is XML wrapped in a `<policies>` element with four child sections: `<inbound>` (statements applied to the request), `<backend>` (applied right before forwarding to the backend), `<outbound>` (applied to the response), and `<on-error>` (run only if an error occurred). If an error happens during inbound, backend, or outbound processing, any remaining statements in that section are skipped and execution jumps to on-error, where you can inspect `context.LastError` and use `set-body` to customize the error response.

sections.heading: Scopes and the base element
sections.body: Policies can be defined at five scopes, from broadest to narrowest: **global** (all APIs), **workspace**, **product**, **API**, and **operation**. When policies are defined at more than one scope, the `<base/>` element controls inheritance and evaluation order within each section - placing `<base/>` first inherits the parent scope's policies before the current scope's statements run; omitting it discards the parent's policies entirely for that section. Note that policies configured at product scope are not applied to requests made with an API-scoped, all-APIs-scoped, or the built-in all-access subscription key.

sections.heading: Rate limiting and quota policies
sections.body: **Limit call rate by subscription** (`rate-limit`) and **set usage quota by subscription** (`quota`) require a subscription key and are available on all gateway types including Consumption. **Limit call rate by key** (`rate-limit-by-key`) and **set usage quota by key** (`quota-by-key`) throttle per an arbitrary calculated key instead, but are *not* available on the Consumption tier. **Limit concurrency** caps how many requests can execute an enclosed policy block at once, and is available across all gateway types.

sections.heading: Authentication policies - what managed identity can and can't do
sections.body: The `authentication-managed-identity` policy uses APIM's system-assigned or a specified user-assigned managed identity to obtain an Entra ID access token for a target `resource` (e.g., `https://vault.azure.net`, `https://storage.azure.com`, `https://servicebus.azure.net`), caches it until expiry, and sets it in the `Authorization: Bearer` header sent to the backend. Its scope is inbound-section authentication to a backend API - it does **not** fetch a TLS/client certificate from Key Vault or configure mutual TLS; that's a separate certificate-management concern. Token forwarding to the correct backend is the caller's responsibility; APIM doesn't validate which backend receives the token.

sections.heading: Caching policies
sections.body: `cache-lookup` (used in inbound) checks for a valid cached response and returns it if present, avoiding a backend call; `cache-store` (used in outbound) caches the response per the specified cache-control configuration. Both are supported across all gateway types (classic, V2, consumption, self-hosted, workspace), alongside key/value cache policies (`cache-lookup-value`, `cache-store-value`, `cache-remove-value`) for storing arbitrary items.

articles.title: Event Grid: Push/Pull Delivery, CloudEvents Schema, and Filtering
articles.summary: Understand Event Grid's pub/sub model for discrete events - schema, topics/subscriptions, filtering, and delivery guarantees.
keyPoints: Event Grid is a fully managed publish-subscribe service for discrete event notifications, using CloudEvents 1.0 (JSON over HTTP) as its preferred schema, plus a proprietary Event Grid schema for some system publishers
Maximum event size is 1 MB; events over 64 KB are billed in 64-KB increments
Supports both push delivery (Event Grid sends events to a configured endpoint) and pull delivery (subscribers connect and read, supported for namespace topics)
Three kinds of topics: custom topics (your own apps), system topics (built-in, e.g. Storage/Event Hubs/Service Bus), and partner topics (external SaaS/ERP)
Event subscriptions define the handler/destination and can filter by event type or subject; subscriptions can be given an expiration date
Push delivery retries failed webhook deliveries for up to 24 hours with exponential backoff until a 200 OK is returned
Common handlers include webhooks, Azure Functions, Event Hubs, Storage Queues, Service Bus, and Logic Apps

sections.heading: Push vs. pull delivery
sections.body: With **push delivery**, you define a destination on an event subscription and Event Grid sends events to it (webhook or Azure service). With **pull delivery** (available for namespace topics), subscriber applications connect to Event Grid to read events on their own schedule, and can release an already-read event back to the broker for later redelivery. Choose pull delivery when you need full control over consumption timing, need private link connectivity, or can't expose a public endpoint; choose push delivery to avoid polling or when your app can't make outbound calls but can receive events on a public endpoint.

sections.heading: Event schema
sections.body: Event Grid's preferred format is the CNCF **CloudEvents 1.0** specification using the HTTP protocol binding and JSON format (structured content mode; binary mode is not supported). It also supports a proprietary **Event Grid schema** used by some system-event publishers. The maximum allowed event size is **1 MB**, and events larger than 64 KB are charged in 64-KB increments. When publishing to a custom topic, events must always be sent as an array (a batch of one is fine for low-throughput cases).

sections.heading: Topics and event subscriptions
sections.body: A **topic** holds published events. **Custom topics** expose their own endpoint for your applications; **system topics** are built-in topics provided by Azure services like Storage, Event Hubs, and Service Bus; **partner topics** surface events from an external SaaS/ERP partner via the Partner Events feature. An **event subscription** tells Event Grid which events on a topic you want and where to send them (a webhook or Azure service resource); subscriptions can be given an expiration time so short-lived test subscriptions clean themselves up automatically.

sections.heading: Filtering and handlers
sections.body: Event subscriptions can filter delivered events by event type or by event subject (advanced filters go further, matching on arbitrary event properties). Supported push-delivery handlers include webhooks and Azure services such as Azure Functions, Event Hubs, Storage Queues, Service Bus, and Logic Apps; the delivery-guarantee mechanism depends on the handler type - for HTTP webhooks, Event Grid retries until it gets a 200 OK; for Storage Queues, it retries until the message push into the queue succeeds.

sections.heading: Reliability
sections.body: If Event Grid can't confirm a subscriber's endpoint received an event via push delivery, it redelivers the event using a retry policy with exponential backoff for up to **24 hours**. This makes Event Grid well suited to reactive, event-driven, serverless architectures where occasional at-least-once delivery and eventual consistency are acceptable.

articles.title: Event Hubs: Partitions, Consumer Groups, Capture, and Retention Limits by Tier
articles.summary: Learn how Event Hubs scales high-throughput streaming with partitions, consumer groups, throughput/processing/capacity units, and exactly how long each tier retains data.
keyPoints: Event Hubs is a fully managed, Kafka-compatible, big-data streaming/ingestion platform supporting AMQP 1.0, Kafka, and HTTPS
Core components: namespace, event hub (partitioned append-only log), partitions (scale unit for parallelism), and consumer groups (independent views of the stream for different consumer applications)
Standard/Basic tiers scale via throughput units (TUs); Premium scales via processing units (PUs); Dedicated scales via capacity units (CUs)
Confirmed retention limits by tier: Basic = 1 day, Standard = 7 days, Premium = 90 days, Dedicated = 90 days
Consumer groups per event hub by tier: Basic = 1, Standard = 20, Premium = 100 (max 200 per PU at namespace level), Dedicated = 1,000 (no limit per CU)
Max published event size by tier: Basic 256 KB, Standard/Premium 1 MB, Dedicated 20 MB

Capture automatically writes streaming data to Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage in Avro format on a time/size window, without consuming TU/PU egress quota; it's included free in Premium/Dedicated, priced separately (hourly) in Standard, and not available (N/A) in Basic

sections.heading: Core components
sections.body: A **namespace** is a management container for one or more event hubs, handling streaming capacity, network security, and geo-DR. An **event hub** (or Kafka topic) is an append-only distributed log split into **partitions** - ordered, independently consumed sequences of events that scale throughput (more partitions = more parallel consumers, like more lanes on a freeway). A **consumer group** is a logical view of the event hub that lets multiple independent consumer applications each read the full stream and track their own offset/checkpoint position.

sections.heading: Scaling: throughput units, processing units, capacity units
sections.body: In the **Basic/Standard** tiers you provision **throughput units (TUs)**; in **Premium** you provision **processing units (PUs)**; in **Dedicated** you get **capacity units (CUs)** for a single-tenant cluster. Per-tier throughput per unit for Basic/Standard is 1 MB/sec or 1,000 events/sec ingress, 2 MB/sec or 4,096 events/sec egress; Premium and Dedicated have no fixed per-unit limit (bounded instead by partitions, storage, and resource allocation).

sections.heading: Data retention and storage by tier
sections.body: Per the official Event Hubs quotas page, the **maximum retention period** is: **Basic = 1 day**, **Standard = 7 days**, **Premium = 90 days**, **Dedicated = 90 days**. Underlying event storage for retention is 84 GB per TU (Basic/Standard), 1 TB per PU (Premium), and 10 TB per CU (Dedicated). Consumer groups per event hub also scale by tier: Basic allows only 1, Standard 20, Premium 100 (capped at 200 per PU namespace-wide), and Dedicated 1,000 per event hub with no per-CU limit.

sections.heading: Capture feature
sections.body: Event Hubs **Capture** automatically writes streaming data to an Azure Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage account in **Apache Avro** format, without requiring you to write any capture code. You configure a capture window using a minimum time interval and size threshold; whichever condition (time or size) is met first triggers the write - a "first wins" policy. Capture reads directly from Event Hubs' internal storage, so it bypasses TU/PU egress quotas entirely, preserving egress budget for real-time readers like Stream Analytics or Spark. Billing-wise, Capture is **included** in Premium and Dedicated, **priced separately per throughput-unit-hour** in Standard, and **not available (N/A)** in Basic.

sections.heading: When to choose Event Hubs
sections.body: Event Hubs is the right choice for high-throughput, time-ordered event streaming - telemetry, application logs, clickstreams, financial transaction streams - where the data model is an ordered stream rather than discrete events (Event Grid) or high-value transactional messages (Service Bus). It supports pub/sub via consumer groups but has no built-in dead-lettering, duplicate detection, or transactions - those are Service Bus strengths.

articles.title: Service Bus: Queues vs. Topics, Sessions, Duplicate Detection, and Dead-Lettering
articles.summary: Master Service Bus's enterprise messaging features - pub/sub topics, FIFO sessions, duplicate detection, and the difference between automatic and application-driven dead-lettering.
keyPoints: Service Bus queues are point-to-point; topics/subscriptions provide 1:n publish-subscribe, with each subscription optionally filtered by rules/actions
Message sessions provide FIFO ordering and let you implement stateful, multiplexed workflows and request-response patterns
Duplicate detection (sender-side, based on message ID within a configurable time window) removes doubt when a send's outcome is uncertain

Dead-lettering is automatic in specific cases (TTL expiration, exceeding the max delivery count - default 10, or exceeding 4 forwarding hops) and can also be triggered explicitly by application code (DeadLetterMessageAsync)
Every queue and subscription has its own dead-letter sub-queue (DLQ) automatically - it doesn't need to be created and has no automatic cleanup
There's also a separate transfer dead-letter queue (TDLQ) for messages that fail during auto-forwarding or send-via
Choose Service Bus over Queue Storage when you need FIFO ordering, duplicate detection, transactions, sessions, pub/sub, or larger messages (up to 100 MB on Premium)

sections.heading: Queues vs. topics and subscriptions
sections.body: **Queues** support point-to-point communication with competing consumers safely obtaining exclusive ownership of messages. **Topics** enable publish-subscribe: a topic can have multiple independent, durable **subscriptions**, each of which behaves like a queue from the receiver's side. A subscription can define **rules** with a filter (a SQL-like condition selecting which messages get copied into it) and an optional **action** that annotates message metadata as it passes through.

sections.heading: Sessions and transactions
sections.body: **Message sessions** provide a first-in-first-out (FIFO) guarantee and let you implement high-scale coordination of workflows or request-response patterns by grouping related messages under a session ID; consuming nodes compete for whole sessions rather than individual messages. Service Bus also supports **transactions** that group multiple operations (e.g., receive from one queue, send to others, complete the original) into a single atomic scope against entities within the same namespace.

sections.heading: Duplicate detection
sections.body: If a client can't be sure whether a send succeeded (e.g., after a timeout), **duplicate detection** lets it safely resend the same message: Service Bus discards duplicate copies based on the message ID within a configurable detection time window. This is a Service Bus-only capability - Queue Storage has no equivalent.

sections.heading: Dead-lettering: automatic vs. explicit
sections.body: The **dead-letter queue (DLQ)** is a secondary sub-queue that exists automatically for every queue and subscription - you don't create or delete it independently, and there's no automatic cleanup of its contents. Messages land there **automatically** when: the message's TTL expires (reason `TTLExpiredException`), delivery is attempted more than the **max delivery count** (default 10, reason `MaxDeliveryCountExceeded`), or (in auto-forward chains) more than 4 forwarding hops occur (`MaxTransferHopCountExceeded`). Applications can also **explicitly** dead-letter a message they can't process by calling `ServiceBusReceiver.DeadLetterMessageAsync`. A related but distinct **transfer dead-letter queue (TDLQ)** holds messages that fail during auto-forwarding or send-via because the destination is disabled, deleted, or over its size limit.

sections.heading: Service Bus vs. Queue Storage
sections.body: Prefer Service Bus when you need guaranteed FIFO ordering (via sessions), automatic duplicate detection, transactional sends/receives, role-based per-sender/receiver permissions, publish-subscribe fan-out, or messages larger than 64 KB (up to 256 KB/1 MB/100 MB depending on tier). Prefer Queue Storage when your queue must exceed 80 GB, you want built-in server-side transaction logs, or you just need simple, high-capacity asynchronous decoupling without the advanced messaging feature set.

articles.title: Queue Storage: Visibility Timeout, TTL, and When Simplicity Beats Service Bus
articles.summary: Learn Azure Queue Storage's simple message model - visibility timeout, TTL, dequeue count - and when its simplicity and scale beat Service Bus's advanced features.
keyPoints: Queue Storage is part of an Azure Storage account: messages up to 64 KB, a queue can hold millions of messages up to the storage account's capacity limit
Get Messages retrieves up to a maximum of 32 messages per call (default is 1 if not specified)
Default visibility timeout is 30 seconds; it must be at least 1 second and cannot exceed 7 days
Default message TTL is 7 days; since REST API version 2017-07-29, TTL can be set to any positive value or -1 to never expire
DequeueCount increments every time a message is retrieved - applications use it to detect and route 'poison' messages manually since Queue Storage has no automatic dead-lettering
Delivery guarantee is at-least-once with no ordering guarantee (a crashed worker can let a visibility timeout expire and the message can be picked up out of order)
Consider Queue Storage when you need >80 GB of queued messages, need server-side transaction logs, or just need simple, low-cost asynchronous decoupling

sections.heading: Basic queue model
sections.body: Azure Queue Storage is accessed via `https://<account>.queue.core.windows.net/<queue>` using authenticated HTTP/HTTPS calls. A **message** can be any content up to **64 KB** (48 KB if Base64-encoded); a single **queue** may hold millions of messages, up to the overall capacity of the storage account. It's a straightforward Web-Queue-Worker style backlog mechanism, not a full messaging broker.

sections.heading: Visibility timeout and message lifecycle
sections.body: When a consumer calls **Get Messages**, it can retrieve up to a maximum of **32 messages** per call (default 1), and each returned message becomes invisible to other consumers for the **visibility timeout** duration - default **30 seconds**, must be ≥1 second and cannot exceed **7 days**. The consumer must delete the message (using its `MessageId` and `PopReceipt`) before the timeout elapses, or the message reappears in the queue for another consumer to pick up - this is why Queue Storage offers no ordering guarantee.

sections.heading: Message TTL and poison-message handling
sections.body: Messages have a **time-to-live**; the default is 7 days, but for REST API version 2017-07-29 or later you can set any positive TTL value or **-1** to mean the message never expires. Because Queue Storage has no built-in dead-lettering, applications detect **poison messages** manually by inspecting the `DequeueCount` property (incremented each time the message is retrieved) and moving messages past an application-defined threshold to their own dead-letter queue.

sections.heading: When Queue Storage beats Service Bus
sections.body: Favor Queue Storage when your application must store more than 80 GB of messages in a single queue, you want to track fine-grained per-message processing progress via in-place message updates, or you need detailed server-side transaction logs of all queue operations for auditing/debugging. It's also simpler and typically cheaper when you don't need Service Bus's FIFO sessions, duplicate detection, transactions, or pub/sub topics.

articles.title: Blob Types and the Blob Storage Client Library Object Model
articles.summary: Covers the three blob types Azure Storage supports, the client library's three-level resource hierarchy with its matching .NET client classes, and the core create/upload/download/copy operations used to perform data operations with the SDK.
keyPoints: Azure Storage supports three blob types: block blobs (text/binary data built from independently managed blocks, can store up to about 190.7 TiB), append blobs (built like block blobs but optimized for append-only operations, e.g. logging data from VMs), and page blobs (random-access files up to 8 TiB, used to store VHD files and serve as disks for Azure VMs).

The client library mirrors Blob Storage's three-level resource hierarchy with three main .NET classes: BlobServiceClient represents the storage account, BlobContainerClient represents a container in that account, and BlobClient represents a single blob in a container.

Container names must be 3-63 characters long, start with a letter or number, and contain only lowercase letters, numbers, and the dash character (no two consecutive dashes) — the name becomes part of the container's URI.

Typical operations: BlobContainerClient.Create/CreateAsync creates a container; container.GetBlobClient(name) obtains a BlobClient; BlobClient.Upload/UploadAsync uploads data (e.g. from a file path or stream) and BlobClient.DownloadTo/DownloadToAsync downloads it; BlobContainerClient.GetBlobs/GetBlobsAsync enumerates the blobs in a container.

Copying a blob server-side is done by calling StartCopyFromUriAsync on the destination BlobClient, passing the source blob's URI. This starts an asynchronous copy and returns a CopyFromUriOperation, so completion must be checked afterwards via the destination blob's GetPropertiesAsync().Value.CopyStatus rather than assumed to happen immediately.

All Blob service operations throw a RequestFailedException (carrying a documented ErrorCode) on failure, and every client instance method is guaranteed thread-safe, so reusing a single client instance — even across threads — is the recommended, safe pattern.

sections.heading: Three blob types
sections.body: Azure Storage supports three types of blobs, and choosing the right one for a scenario is a recurring exam theme. Block blobs store text and binary data as a set of blocks that can be managed (uploaded, replaced) individually; they're the default choice for documents, images, and media, and can store up to about 190.7 TiB. Append blobs are also composed of blocks like block blobs, but they're optimized specifically for append operations — the canonical scenario is logging data from virtual machines, where new data is only ever added to the end of the blob. Page blobs store random-access files up to 8 TiB in size and are the blob type used to store VHD (virtual hard drive) files, serving as the backing disks for Azure virtual machines.

sections.heading: Resource hierarchy and client classes
sections.body: Blob Storage exposes three resource levels: the storage account, a container within the account, and a blob within a container. The Azure.Storage.Blobs client library for .NET mirrors this exactly with three client classes. BlobServiceClient represents the storage account itself and is the entry point for account-level operations (e.g., listing containers). BlobContainerClient represents a single container and is obtained either by constructing it directly or via BlobServiceClient.GetBlobContainerClient(name); it's used for container-level operations such as Create/Delete and for obtaining blob clients. BlobClient represents a single blob and is obtained via BlobContainerClient.GetBlobClient(name); it exposes the actual data operations (upload, download, properties, metadata). Container names are constrained because they become part of the container's URI: 3-63 characters, must start with a letter or number, and can only contain lowercase letters, numbers, and dashes (never two dashes in a row).

sections.heading: Core operations: create, upload, download, enumerate
sections.body: A typical workflow creates a BlobContainerClient (from a connection string and container name, or from a BlobServiceClient), calls Create/CreateAsync to ensure the container exists, then calls container.GetBlobClient(blobName) to get a BlobClient for a specific blob. Uploading is done via BlobClient.Upload/UploadAsync — commonly from a local file path or a Stream — and downloading via BlobClient.DownloadTo/DownloadToAsync to a local path or stream. To enumerate the blobs already in a container, BlobContainerClient.GetBlobs/GetBlobsAsync returns BlobItem entries (exposing at least the blob's Name) without needing to know their names in advance. Every synchronous method has an async counterpart, and all client instance methods are documented as thread-safe, so a single long-lived client instance can safely be shared and reused across the application rather than re-created per call.

sections.heading: Copying a blob server-side
sections.body: The most efficient way to copy a blob from one container (or account) to another is a server-side copy rather than downloading and re-uploading the bytes through the client application. This is initiated by calling StartCopyFromUriAsync on the destination BlobClient, passing the source blob's Uri — i.e., the call is made on the target blob, referencing the source, not the other way around. The operation begins an asynchronous copy on the service side and returns a CopyFromUriOperation describing the copy's state; because the copy isn't guaranteed to be complete when the call returns, the actual completion must be confirmed by calling GetPropertiesAsync() on the destination blob and inspecting the returned BlobProperties.CopyStatus. On failure, Blob service operations throw a RequestFailedException with a specific ErrorCode (or an AggregateException if multiple failures occurred), which is the mechanism application code should catch to handle recoverable errors such as a container already existing or already being deleted.

articles.title: Application Map: Visualizing Distributed Topology and Mapping OpenTelemetry Span Kinds to Requests vs Dependencies
articles.summary: Explains how Application Map discovers and displays your distributed application's components and dependency calls, how to filter and troubleshoot it, and the OpenTelemetry span-kind rule that decides whether a span shows up as a Request or a Dependency.
keyPoints: Application Map represents application topology as nodes (components, identified by their cloud role name/roleName property) connected by directional edges (dependency calls from a source node to a target node); it's built by following HTTP dependency calls between instrumented components.

Components are independently deployable parts of your app that you have code/telemetry access to; they're distinct from 'observed' external dependencies (e.g. Azure SQL, Event Hubs) which your team doesn't instrument directly. Components can be different roles reporting to one Application Insights resource, or separate Application Insights resources entirely (even across subscriptions).

The map is built by progressive discovery: on first load a query discovers components related to the main one, and 'Update map components' re-runs discovery to refresh all nodes - this isn't needed when every component is just a different role inside a single Application Insights resource.

Cloud role instance (separate from cloud role name) lets you drill into a specific load-balanced server/instance behind a node - useful to tell whether a problem affects all instances of a role or just one; it can be overridden via OpenTelemetry resource attributes, or via JavaScript telemetry initializers for browser telemetry.

Node filters (Nodes only / Nodes and sources / Nodes and targets / Nodes, sources and targets, with contains/!contains/==/!= operators) and connector filters (by error state, error rate, average call duration, or call count, with Pxx percentile-based values) let you cut down a noisy map to a focused view, and can be pinned to a dashboard.

Intelligent view applies a machine-learning model (trained on the map's historical behavior) to highlight only the edges most likely to be the root cause of a failure, filtering out 'benign' failure noise in large distributed apps; sensitivity is adjustable (High/Medium/Low) and it supports time windows up to 7 days.

For .NET (System.Diagnostics.Activity/ActivitySource), ActivityKind.Client, ActivityKind.Producer, and ActivityKind.Internal are mapped to Application Insights 'dependencies', while ActivityKind.Server and ActivityKind.Consumer are mapped to Application Insights 'requests'. StartActivity defaults to ActivityKind.Internal if no kind is specified.

For Java, the OpenTelemetry @WithSpan annotation defaults to populating the 'dependencies' table with dependency type InProc; for a background job not captured by autoinstrumentation that should count as an operation (e.g. appear in the Requests table), you must explicitly set kind = SpanKind.SERVER on the @WithSpan annotation.

sections.heading: Nodes, connectors, and what counts as a component
sections.body: Application Map draws circles (*nodes*) for each application component or its dependencies, and directional lines (*connectors*/*edges*) for the HTTP calls between a *source* node and a *target* node. Nodes are identified by the component's cloud role name (roleName) property in recorded telemetry. A **component** is a part of your distributed/microservice app that your team can see code or telemetry for; it's different from an *observed external dependency* like Azure SQL Database or Event Hubs, which you typically don't instrument directly. Components can be separate roles reporting into a single Application Insights resource, or entirely separate Application Insights resources (even across subscriptions) - Application Map stitches the topology together either way, as long as you have access to each resource.

sections.heading: Discovery, cloud role instances, and filtering a noisy map
sections.body: The map is populated by *progressive discovery*: the initial load runs a query to find components related to the main one, and a status bar tracks how many components have been found so far; the **Update map components** action re-triggers discovery to refresh the full node set (not required when every component is just a different role inside one Application Insights resource - the initial load already finds those). When a role has multiple load-balanced instances, the **cloud role instance** property (separate from cloud role name) lets you investigate whether an issue is affecting one specific instance or all of them; override it via OpenTelemetry resource attributes for server apps, or JavaScript telemetry initializers for browser apps. To cut a large map down to size, **node filters** (search node properties with contains/!contains/==/!= across Nodes only / Nodes and sources / Nodes and targets / Nodes, sources and targets) and **connector filters** (by error state, error rate, average call duration, or call count - several of which use Pxx percentile values) can be combined and pinned to a dashboard, e.g. an 'Error connector' filter to permanently watch for red (failing) edges.

sections.heading: Intelligent view: ML-assisted root-cause highlighting
sections.body: In large distributed apps, ordinary failure-rate coloring can make Application Map noisy with many red edges from low-impact, 'benign' failures. **Intelligent view** applies a machine-learning model trained on the map's historical behavior to highlight, in red, only the edges that are the most probable causes of a service failure, and it surfaces actionable insights explaining why a given edge was flagged. Detection sensitivity is adjustable - High highlights fewer edges, Medium is the balanced default, Low highlights more - and Intelligent view supports time windows of up to 7 days; it may take a minute to load for very large applications.

sections.heading: OpenTelemetry span kinds decide Request vs Dependency
sections.body: Whichever telemetry type a span becomes in Application Insights (and therefore how it's classified in the Requests table vs the Dependencies table) is governed by its OpenTelemetry span kind, not by where the code runs. In .NET, `ActivitySource.StartActivity()` defaults to `ActivityKind.Internal` if you don't pass a kind explicitly. `ActivityKind.Client`, `ActivityKind.Producer`, and `ActivityKind.Internal` are all mapped to Application Insights **dependencies**, while only `ActivityKind.Server` and `ActivityKind.Consumer` are mapped to Application Insights **requests** - so a worker that merely processes a message (e.g. pulled from Azure Service Bus) needs to be started as a Server or Consumer-kind span/activity to show up as a Request rather than a Dependency. In Java, the `@WithSpan` annotation defaults to the Dependencies table with dependency type `InProc`; for a background job not otherwise captured by autoinstrumentation that you want treated as an operation (appearing in Requests), you must explicitly set `kind = SpanKind.SERVER` on the annotation.
